Text | Er Mu

Editing | Er Mu, Fanyu Meng

Since Minor Heat, the solar term that marks the start of high summer in the Chinese calendar, it has got seriously hot. The whole Northern Hemisphere is a furnace!

Just look at the recent news:

Camels in Algeria are fainting from the heat in the Sahara!

Canada’s west coast has broken its all-time temperature record, and mussels are cooking to death on the shore!

Highways in Washington State are cracking in the heat!

A man in Dongguan, in southern China, had his flip-flops melt!

Your editor, swamped with work lately, has been laid low by the heat too, but to keep our posting streak alive I dragged myself up to keep typing. And what writer’s companion, what cure for the summer heat, beats an ice-cold watermelon? So, faster than a speeding bull in a china shop, I went downstairs, out of the housing complex, to the fruit shop on the corner and made straight for the watermelon stand. The street was bustling with people coming and going, and I stood frowning at a heap of melons. How on earth do you choose? As I hesitated, an auntie with the air of vast life experience stepped over and, without a moment’s pause, launched into a percussion performance: pfft-pfft, tock-tock, thunk-thunk… After a flurry of drumming, she decisively picked up the one she liked and headed for the till. I watched her disappear into the crowd, my eyes shining with admiration!

(The above is based on a true story.)

When buying a watermelon, plenty of people habitually give it a few slaps and listen to the sound to judge its quality. Some really can hear a difference; others probably just slap away out of habit, to look like they know what they’re doing. So is there any science behind judging a watermelon by its sound?

Of course there is! The principle is that the way sound waves travel through a medium depends on the medium’s density and texture.

A watermelon consists mainly of rind and flesh. As it ripens, the structural properties of the rind, such as its hardness and elastic modulus, change. The riper the melon, the more elastic the rind, so it springs back slightly when you slap it. In the flesh, cellulase breaks down the cellulose, and the sugar content and structure change as well. So a watermelon sounds different when tapped at different stages of ripeness.

Put simply, an unripe watermelon is denser and sounds crisper when tapped; a ripe one is less dense and sounds duller. A clear, crisp “tock” probably means an unripe melon; a muddy, dull “thunk” most likely means a ripe one; and a “pfft” may mean an overripe melon (one with a hollow heart).

Acoustic signals from unripe, ripe and overripe watermelons

Watermelon quality can be characterized mainly by four parameters: soluble solids content, maturity (ripeness), firmness, and internal defects (hollow heart). When sound waves hit a watermelon, they are reflected or transmitted. Analyzing the reflected or transmitted waves yields a set of acoustic features, such as the attenuation coefficient, propagation velocity, acoustic impedance and natural frequency. These acoustic parameters are related to the quality parameters, and once the relationship between the two sets has been worked out, the quality of a watermelon can be judged by analyzing the sound it makes when tapped.

Most research in this area is about pinning down that relationship. Let’s see what interesting things these “bored” researchers have come up with.

A quick search turns up quite a lot:

A portable device for measuring watermelon firmness, developed by Sugiyama et al. in 1998. It consists essentially of a mechanical tapper and two microphones.

d.

A watermelon tester from the Japanese company AVA, based on spectral analysis, used mainly to judge ripeness and detect hollow heart.

Of course, no relationship-hunting job these days is complete without machine learning. And with smartphones growing explosively more powerful, one researcher (Zeng, 2014) combined the two into a phone app that identifies good melons with 89% accuracy.

All right, all right. All these technical terms, clever algorithms and precision instruments look very impressive, but sometimes reality looks like this:

The scientists may bring their gadgets galore, but one auntie’s drum solo still settles the score!

“When will science finally beat the auntie?”

Besides listening, here are four more tips for picking a watermelon:

1. Check the stem

Choose one with a dry stem, not a green, moist one.

2. Check the color of the spot where it lay on the ground

Choose an orange-yellow spot, not a white one.

3. Tell “female” from “male”

Round “female” melons are sweeter than long, oval “male” ones.

4. Check the webbing

If the rind has a netlike webbing, choose the melon where it covers a larger area.

Reference: Tong et al., “Research advances in nondestructive determination of internal quality in watermelon/melon: A review”
